articles.title: Calculating WAL Generation for DML Operations in PostgreSQL
articles.excerpt: PostgreSQL provides the EXPLAIN command with the ANALYZE and WAL options to measure the WAL generated by a DML operation. This feature helps database administrators investigate the impact of INSERT, U…
articles.body: PostgreSQL provides the EXPLAIN command with the ANALYZE and WAL options to measure the WAL generated by a DML operation. This feature helps database administrators investigate the impact of INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements on WAL generation. In this article, we use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL) to measure the WAL generated when updating 10 million rows, compare the results with and without an index, and investigate the effect of enabling WAL compression. 1. Test environment The test uses a person table containing 10 million rows . The table occupies approximately 880 MB , and WAL compression is initially disabled.

articles.title: AI to Human Handoff Template: The 5 Fields That End Repeats
articles.excerpt: Routing decides who answers. The handoff decides what they know when they open the thread. Five fields turn a six-minute reconstruction into a sixty-second reply, and stop the customer repeating thems…
articles.body: Routing decides who answers. The handoff decides what they know when they open the thread. Five fields turn a six-minute reconstruction into a sixty-second reply, and stop the customer repeating themselves a third time. A property-management company with 340 units put an AI agent on its tenant chat line. A tenant wrote in about a slow leak under the kitchen sink, explained that maintenance had already visited once and rescheduled, and added the two windows when they'd be home. The agent recognized the escalation trigger and handed off in under a second. Technically flawless. Then the human opened the thread and typed: "Hi, how can I help you today?" The tenant, who had now explained the same leak three times to three surfaces, closed the chat and wrote the review instead.

articles.title: Scale-to-Zero vs Provisioned Managed Postgres: Which Pricing Model Fits Your Traffic?
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: Scale-to-zero Postgres (billed mostly on compute time actually used) wins when your database is idle most of the day, such as side projects, staging, and per-PR previews. A provisioned instance…
articles.body: TL;DR: Scale-to-zero Postgres (billed mostly on compute time actually used) wins when your database is idle most of the day, such as side projects, staging, and per-PR previews. A provisioned instance (billed per hour whether or not anyone queries it) wins once your database is busy for a large fraction of the month, because you stop paying a premium for elasticity you no longer use. The break-even is a ratio of active hours to total hours, and you can compute it in ten lines of code with your own provider's current rates. I'm deliberately not publishing a price table. Rates change, and a stale number in a reference post does more harm than none. What lasts is the shape of each billing model, and that shape is what decides your bill.

articles.title: A traceability import should never guess a missing lot code
articles.excerpt: A supplier sends a CSV of shipping rows. Row 37 has no traceability lot code. The importer has three choices: reject the row, store it with a warning, or fill the gap with something like UNKNOWN so th…
articles.body: A supplier sends a CSV of shipping rows. Row 37 has no traceability lot code. The importer has three choices: reject the row, store it with a warning, or fill the gap with something like UNKNOWN so the batch goes through. The third option feels friendliest on upload day and does the most damage during a trace request. This post is about where to draw that line for FSMA 204 records, the FDA food traceability rule. The pattern applies to any import where a missing field can quietly turn into a wrong answer later. What a shipping record has to carry For foods on the Food Traceability List, the rule names key data elements (KDEs) for each critical tracking event (CTE).

articles.title: ISO 42001 não é lei em país nenhum, mas o cliente já cobra como se fosse
articles.excerpt: ISO 42001 não é lei em país nenhum, mas o cliente já cobra como se fosse O problema Nenhum país tornou a ISO/IEC 42001 obrigatória por lei. Não o Brasil, não a União Europeia. E ainda assim a pergunta…
articles.body: ISO 42001 não é lei em país nenhum, mas o cliente já cobra como se fosse O problema Nenhum país tornou a ISO/IEC 42001 obrigatória por lei. Não o Brasil, não a União Europeia. E ainda assim a pergunta "isso é obrigatório?" aparece cada vez mais em reunião de diretoria. Eu audito sistemas críticos sob SOX, ITIL e LGPD há quase vinte anos, e vejo o mesmo padrão se repetir com toda norma nova: ela é voluntária no papel, e quem cobra na prática não é o legislador. São três fontes de pressão diferentes, e misturá-las leva a duas decisões ruins: ignorar o assunto porque "não é lei ainda", ou certificar às pressas achando que isso resolve uma obrigação legal que nem existe. O que já é obrigatório, com ou sem ISO 42001 A LGPD trata de decisão automatizada desde que entrou em vigor, no artigo 20.

articles.body: Every developer building a Micro-SaaS runs into the same wall: before you can monetize your core AI value proposition, you need to spend 40+ hours wiring up the exact same commodity infrastructure. You write authentication middleware, implement password hashing, configure database migrations, stand up REST endpoints for basic CRUD, wire rate limiters, and connect AI queues. By the time you are ready to test product-market fit, you've burned two weeks writing code that does not differentiate your product in any way. In this guide, we will break down how to bypass traditional backend infrastructure entirely by turning n8n into a full-scale, headless Micro-SaaS engine equipped with JWT authentication, internal data management, and an asynchronous AI generation pipeline. 1.

articles.title: The 'Halloween Fireballs' are coming. Here's what to expect from the Taurids this year
articles.excerpt: The Southern and Northern Taurid meteor showers will produce occasional bright, slow-moving meteors worldwide during October and November, with moon-free peaks in 2026.
articles.body: They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs. The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it. The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 12, 1964: The Soviet Union launches Voskhod 1, the 1st multi-person cosmonaut crew, into space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight . This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft. Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits . Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space. On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched the first multiperson mission, Voskhod 1, which launched three Russian cosmonauts into space.

articles.body: "Tomb Raider" celebrates its 30th anniversary this month. While many remember the iconic T-Rex or locking Winston the Butler in the freezer, many forget about the UFO in 1998’s "Tomb Raider III"; a mysterious alien craft that worked a lot like Doctor Who ’s TARDIS. Coming off the back of the hugely successful "Tomb Raider 2", developer Core Design had big plans for the third entry, including kayaking, those iconic London levels, and, of course, a level featuring a UFO in Area 51. Although it looked small on the outside, the UFO featured multiple floors for players to explore as they searched for a vital artifact, all as enemies swarmed in.

articles.title: What caused a mysterious atmospheric explosion in Siberia in 1908?
articles.excerpt: Fire erupted in the morning skies over Siberia on June 30, 1908, as an atmospheric explosion occurred that remains unmatched by any similar event in modern history.
articles.body: Fire erupted in the morning skies over Siberia on June 30, 1908, as an atmospheric explosion occurred that remains unmatched by any similar event in modern history. That day, at approximately 7:15 a.m. local time, observers in Siberia's remote Tunguska region became witnesses to the entry of a brilliant fireball into Earth's atmosphere , trailing smoke across the dawn sky and culminating in a flash brighter than the sun itself. Within seconds, the explosion and resulting shock waves that followed reportedly knocked some members of the nearby Indigenous Evenki population off their feet, and caused damage to dwellings and livestock, while seismic instruments hundreds of miles away logged tremors caused by the blast.
articles.author: Micah Hanks

articles.title: UAE unveils lander for bold 7-asteroid mission set to launch in 2028 (photos)
articles.excerpt: In March 2028, the UAE is set to launch an ambitious mission to the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter that will culminate with a landing attempt on a mysteriously reddish space rock.
articles.body: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has moved a step closer to launching its second-ever interplanetary mission — an ambitious, eight-year exploration of seven asteroids between Mars and Jupiter that will culminate with a landing on the mysteriously red asteroid 269 Justitia. The mission team unveiled a half-scale model of the homegrown probe that will make that landing during an Oct. 1 press conference in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE. The autonomous craft will ride attached to the main spacecraft MBR Explorer , named after Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid al-Maktoum, the ruler of Dubai and the UAE's prime minister.
